title: From Extract to Finished Product: Stability, Encapsulation and Regulatory Status of Clitoria ternatea Anthocyanins as a Natural Blue Ingredient
content: Blue is the colour the natural palette does not easily supply, and regulatory pressure to retire petroleum-derived dyes has made the gap commercially urgent. Butterfly pea (Clitoria ternatea L.) is the most credible natural blue available to food and supplement manufacturers, because its pigments are polyacylated anthocyanins, the ternatins, whose long aromatic side chains hold the blue quinonoid base stable across a pH range in which ordinary anthocyanins fail. This review draws the published work together from the formulator’s end rather than the chemist’s: what the pigment does between the extraction vessel and the finished pack. Three conclusions follow. First, the stability optimum is near neutrality, not in acid — the half-life of the blue form at pH 7 and 4 °C is reported at 334 days against 51 days for the flavylium cation at pH 0.5, which inverts the rule of thumb carried over from red anthocyanins and makes beverage pH the single most consequential formulation decision. Second, colour stability and antioxidant capacity do not track together: radical-scavenging activity falls away above pH 7 while visible blue persists to pH 10, so a product that still looks right may no longer carry the activity its positioning claims. Third, encapsulation is now well characterised for this extract, with maltodextrin-based wall systems retaining above 90% of anthocyanins through spray drying, yet almost all of that work reports retention at the point of manufacture rather than through the shelf life of a real matrix. The review also sets out a regulatory asymmetry that the technical literature has largely ignored: butterfly pea flower extract is a listed colour additive in the United States with permitted uses widened in 2025, while in the European Union the dried flower has met a safety objection grounded in its cyclotide content rather than in its pigments. Extract specifications that address only anthocyanin content therefore leave the binding commercial constraint unmeasured.
